name: Trazodone / prescription sleep meds

card.summary: A prescription antidepressant widely used off-label for sleep; evidence for insomnia is modest and there are no appearance studies.
card.note: Prescription-only; adverse effects include sedation, low blood pressure and rare cardiac and priapism events.

quick.overview:
Trazodone is an antidepressant developed in Italy in the 1960s and approved in the US in 1981. Doctors commonly prescribe it at low doses off-label for insomnia, which is how it enters conversations about sleep as a part of looksmaxxing recovery.

Its place in appearance culture is indirect: the premise is that better sleep supports skin, weight and general looks. No published study has tested trazodone or other prescription sleep medicines for any appearance outcome.
quick.mechanism: Trazodone blocks serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and also acts on adrenergic and histamine receptors, with a weak effect on serotonin reuptake. Its sedating action is attributed mainly to these receptor effects rather than to a classic sedative mechanism.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include dry mouth, sedation, headache, orthostatic hypotension, and, rarely, QT prolongation, priapism, mania and liver toxicity. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, and stopping abruptly can cause a discontinuation syndrome.

lead: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant (a serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor) that doctors commonly prescribe at low doses off-label to help people fall and stay asleep. In looksmaxxing and recovery discussions it, along with other prescription sleep medicines, is treated as a medical route to better sleep, which people link to fresher-looking skin and eyes, steadier weight and better training recovery.[1][5]

The appearance link rests on research on sleep itself: a 2010 experimental study at the Karolinska Institute photographed adults after normal sleep and after sleep deprivation, and observers rated the sleep-deprived faces as less healthy, more tired and slightly less attractive.[6] Trazodone is one of several tools used to treat the underlying insomnia; no published study has tested it for appearance outcomes.

Trazodone was developed by Angelini Research Laboratories in Italy in the 1960s, marketed in Italy from 1972 and approved by the US FDA in 1981.[1] Meta-analyses report short-term improvement in sleep measures; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against its use for insomnia.[1][3][4]

chain: Prescribed sedating action helps with falling and staying asleep
Better-rested face, skin, recovery and training
angle.text: People who struggle to sleep discuss trazodone and similar prescription medicines as a way to get regular sleep, which they connect with a fresher look, calmer skin and better recovery. Its use for insomnia is off-label and directed by a prescriber.

paras: The primary approved use is major depressive disorder. Off-label uses include anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, where evidence is limited, and it is often combined with SSRIs [1].

For insomnia, low doses are commonly prescribed off-label [1]. Other prescription sleep medicines discussed alongside it include Z-drugs such as zolpidem and orexin receptor antagonists such as daridorexant.

In the 2010 Karolinska study of 23 adults photographed after a normal night and after sleep deprivation, 65 untrained observers rated sleep-deprived faces as less healthy and more tired, with a small reduction in attractiveness ratings; the authors suggested people are sensitive to facial cues of sleep loss.[6]
This is the basis for the premise in recovery-minded communities that treating insomnia supports how the face and skin look; the studies of trazodone itself measure sleep, not appearance.

Common effects reported include dry mouth, faintness, vomiting, headache and sedation. Serious but less common effects include suicidal ideation (monitoring is advised in young people), mania, irregular heart rhythm or QT prolongation, and priapism. Orthostatic hypotension raises fall risk in older adults, and abrupt cessation can cause a discontinuation syndrome [1].

Trazodone is a potent 5-HT2A antagonist, a weaker 5-HT2C antagonist and a 5-HT1A partial agonist. It also blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, weakly blocks histamine H1 receptors and weakly inhibits serotonin reuptake. It lacks anticholinergic activity [1].
Oral bioavailability is about 63 to 80 percent. The immediate-release half-life is about 4 to 15 hours. It is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 into an active metabolite, mCPP [1].
No studies have examined trazodone or other prescription sleep medicines for appearance outcomes.

For insomnia, a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials compared trazodone with placebo on sleep-related outcomes and safety.[3] A 2017 systematic review of 45 studies reported repeated demonstration of efficacy in primary and secondary insomnia, noting that use at lower doses has become standard since the 2000s.[4] A 2022 network meta-analysis in The Lancet compared pharmacological treatments for acute and long-term insomnia across many drugs.[7] A randomized trial in early Alzheimer's disease (REST) has examined trazodone to improve sleep and cognition.[8] A Cochrane review has described low-to-moderate quality evidence and no long-term data.[1]

Registered trials include a 1,200-person phase 4 trial comparing common prescription and over-the-counter insomnia medications [2] and a 1,000-person phase 4 trial comparing digital therapy, trazodone and daridorexant for menopause-related insomnia.[9] Results have not been published.
Trazodone is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the UK and Australia. Brand names include Desyrel and Trittico worldwide, Molipaxin in the UK and Ireland, and Oleptro in the US [1].

On T Nation, forum members discuss sleep difficulty alongside hormone therapy and training, and list trazodone, Z-drugs, benzodiazepines and sonata among prescription options, with some posters stating that sleep problems warrant a doctor visit.[10][11] One poster says that after fairly heavy use of Ambien and Lunesta they noticed a downside, illustrating mixed user experience with hypnotics.[12]

timeline.event: Developed by Angelini Research Laboratories in Italy [1]
American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline recommends against its use for insomnia [1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, prescription sleep aids come up in threads about insomnia, low energy and hormone therapy, usually as options to raise with a doctor.[10][11][12]

claims.claim: Prescription sleep medicine can fix poor sleep that otherwise drags down energy and recovery.
claims.believers: Posters describe insomnia as a major problem and list trazodone, Z-drugs and benzodiazepines as prescribed options, adding that doctors who prescribe benzodiazepines can generally prescribe trazodone.[11]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report short-term improvements in sleep with trazodone, with low-to-moderate quality evidence and no long-term data; the AASM 2017 guideline recommended against it for insomnia.[1][3][4]

claims.claim: Z-drugs and similar hypnotics can leave users feeling less rested after heavy use.
claims.believers: One poster who used Ambien and Lunesta 3 to 6 nights per week describes a major downside after moderately heavy use.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists sedation, orthostatic hypotension and discontinuation syndrome among trazodone effects; adverse effects differ by drug.[1]
